{
 "summary": "Removes redundant cache invalidation and UI change notifications for parent transactions when wallet outputs are spent. Deletes MarkInputsDirty and stops CommitTransaction from notifying spent parent transactions. Adds unit tests verifying that spending an output, abandoning a spend, or receiving a spend via mempool does not alter parent transaction cached values.",
 "problem": "Previously, CWalletTx cached available amounts, requiring spent parent transactions to invalidate their caches and notify the GUI when their outputs were spent. Following #27286, available balance is computed from separate structures while CWalletTx caches only transaction-specific credit, debit, and change amounts that do not change upon spending, leaving the invalidation and GUI notification logic redundant.",
 "evidence": [
  "Author notes that since #27286, \"the balance is read live from m_txos and mapTxSpends, and CWalletTx cache only its own, tx specific, incoming and outgoing amounts... So the cache invalidation recomputes the same values, and the notification makes the GUI refresh a status that has not changed.\" (PR description)",
  "Commit 4591142a8f notes that the GUI is the only consumer of the notification, and its status refresh depends on depth, maturity, and abandoned flags, none of which change when an output is spent."
 ],

<category name="wallet" title="Wallet">
## Covers

The bitcoind wallet: key and descriptor management, transaction creation
and coin selection, PSBT handling, wallet database (SQLite, and the
legacy BDB migration path), backup and recovery, rescanning, wallet RPCs,
and wallet-facing pieces of the GUI. Fee estimation is wallet when the
change is about how the wallet uses it.

Borderline: a descriptor or PSBT change that affects only `bitcoin-tx` or
RPC without wallet code is rpc, not wallet. An `interfaces::Wallet`
change is both wallet and ipc.

## What matters here

Fund safety first: anything that could lose keys, double-spend
unintentionally, create an unspendable output, or corrupt the wallet
database. Then backup, recovery, and migration correctness, including the
legacy-to-descriptor migration path that every remaining legacy user
must cross. Then privacy of transaction creation (address reuse, change
detection, fingerprinting). Then user-visible reliability: hangs, slow
rescans, confusing failures, wrong balances. Then features users have
asked for, with evidence they have asked.

The rubric does not ask whether Bitcoin Core should have a wallet. It
asks, given that it does, what a wallet user needs most.
